strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation problem in brain-to-text decoding: overlapping stimuli and subjects can make reported performance misleading about generalization. This methodological focus is relevant to NLP independently of whether a new decoding architecture is proposed.

The proposed requirement to hold out both subjects and stimuli is sensible for evaluating their joint generalization. Explicitly accounting for overlapping fMRI windows is a useful practical contribution.

The experiments cover two datasets, two established models, several splitting strategies, additional held-out data, and shuffled inputs. Appendix E also includes comparisons without teacher forcing, providing useful initial evidence that split choice matters beyond teacher-forced evaluation.
weaknesses: The main benchmark does not evaluate autonomous generation. Table 6 identifies the results used in Tables 3–5 as teacher-forced: for example, UniCoRN on ZuCo under the proposed split falls from 23.32 to 14.02 BLEU-1 without teacher forcing. Supplying correct target prefixes materially changes the task. Although Table 6 is useful, the additional-test and shuffled-input controls also need evaluation without teacher forcing, and Table 5 should report the corresponding generation benchmark.

The published algorithms do not enforce the claimed splitting guarantee. Algorithm 1, line 15, adds edges from training subjects without checking whether their text belongs to validation or test. Algorithm 2, line 33, similarly permits held-out subjects to be added through training stories. These steps can reintroduce stimulus and subject overlap, respectively, contradicting Equations 13–14. Corrected pseudocode and audits of the actual experimental splits are necessary.

The leakage metrics are not reproducible from their mathematical definitions. Equation 17 counts identical signal observations appearing in both splits, whereas the stated concept concerns shared subject identity. Disjoint EEG observations can therefore yield zero under this equation despite complete subject overlap; subjects absent from training also create an undefined denominator. Equations 6–7 additionally require overlap for every training example rather than detecting any overlap. These discrepancies undermine the interpretation of Table 2.

Several causal interpretations exceed the evidence. Decreasing validation loss does not establish that encoder representations are degrading, and improving test scores with longer training does not prove leakage. Comparisons across splitting methods also change training-data availability and test subjects or stories. Matched training sizes, a clearly specified common evaluation set, and separate controls for subject and stimulus overlap are needed to attribute performance differences.

Reproducibility details are insufficient for the claimed released benchmark. The manuscript provides no code or split-download link, exact retained and discarded sample counts, or precise construction of the additional test set. The unit of input shuffling is unclear. Four-seed reporting covers leakage rates, while uncertainty across model runs and held-out subjects or stories is absent from decoding results.

Numerical reporting contains material inconsistencies. Narratives method (a) has ROUGE-1 recall 40.65 in Table 7, but the same number is labeled F-score in Table 3. Table 5 reports EEG2Text F-score 25.74 with precision 23.95 and recall 23.98, which is incompatible with standard F-score aggregation over the same examples. These results require correction and verification.

The conclusion that all existing splitting methods make evaluation meaningless is too broad. Joint generalization to unseen subjects and unseen stimuli is a particular evaluation target; transfer to new subjects on known stimuli can also be legitimate when stated accurately. Appendix D's universal claim that samples must be discarded also needs additional assumptions, since disconnected subject–stimulus components can be partitioned intact. Together with the unresolved experimental and implementation issues, these concerns prevent a sound Findings recommendation and motivate resubmission next cycle.
